what_its_for: Cenobamate is a seizure medicine (antiepileptic) used to treat partial-onset seizures in adults. Partial-onset seizures start in one area of the brain and may or may not spread to other parts of the brain.
how_to_take: Take cenobamate by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole. Try to take it at the same time every day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets unless your doctor or pharmacist tells you it is okay.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over several weeks to reduce the chance of a serious allergic reaction. A common starting dose is 12.5 mg once daily for the first two weeks. Your doctor will then increase your dose every two weeks (to 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, then up to 200 mg once daily). Some people may need up to 400 mg once daily. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing schedule — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store cenobamate at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in its original container, tightly closed. Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired tablets safely — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking cenobamate. Alcohol can increase dizziness, sleepiness, and the risk of serious side effects. Be careful driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that require alertness until you know how this medicine affects you — it can cause dizziness and drowsiness. Avoid stopping cenobamate suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause more seizures. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, because cenobamate can interact with many other drugs.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you develop: a skin rash, blistering, peeling skin, or sores in your mouth (signs of a serious allergic reaction called DRESS or Stevens-Johnson Syndrome); fever, swollen lymph nodes, or flu-like symptoms; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); unusual changes in mood, behavior, depression, or thoughts of hurting yourself; severe dizziness, trouble walking, or confusion; or if your seizures get worse or change in type. DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) is a rare but life-threatening reaction — get help immediately if you notice a rash with fever and swollen glands.
when_it_works: Cenobamate works gradually. Because the dose is increased slowly over several weeks, it may take 2 to 3 months before you reach your full dose and notice the maximum benefit. Do not stop taking it because you do not see immediate results — give it time to reach the right level in your body. Keep taking it every day even if you feel well, because stopping suddenly can trigger seizures.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before becoming pregnant. Cenobamate may harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control while taking this medicine. Enroll in the North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) Pregnancy Registry if you become pregnant (1-888-233-2334). Breastfeeding: It is not known if cenobamate passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Older adults (65+): Use with caution — older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and falls. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Cenobamate should not be used in people with a genetic condition called Familial Short QT Syndrome.
